messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh is a 22-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who works as a call center agent and has been married for just over a year. She presented for intake with a PCL-5 score of 61, describing a presentation that has steadily worsened over the past eighteen months following a sexual assault perpetrated by a male supervisor at a previous job. The assault occurred in a back office after a shift; he had called her in under the guise of a performance review. What she remembers of that evening does not arrive as a continuous story — it comes in disconnected pieces that refuse to assemble: the texture of the chair, a particular taste she cannot name but cannot escape, the sound of a door locking. These fragments feel more immediate to her than anything she has experienced since, more real than her wedding day, more vivid than her husband's face at breakfast. She has described them as intrusions that arrive without warning rather than memories she can choose to revisit.

The assault happened in a context saturated with authority, and that saturation has spread outward into her daily life. When Linh encounters anyone in a position of power — a floor supervisor at the call center walking the aisles, a security guard in a parking structure — her body responds before her mind can intervene. She has developed a habit of scanning every room she enters for exits, a reflex so automatic she now does it in her own home. Unexpected movement nearby — a colleague leaning across her desk, her husband reaching past her — triggers a startle response she cannot suppress. She had come to believe that vigilance is the only thing standing between her and another assault; to let her guard down, even briefly, felt to her like an invitation. It was this sustained sense of threat — the body-level certainty that harm was close and that she alone had to prevent it — that drove her toward the strategies she had assembled to survive: deflecting any conversation that edged near the assault, refusing to acknowledge adjacent references, and using sexual fantasy as a way of asserting some ownership over her own body. When the threat felt this immediate, those strategies were not avoidance in any abstract sense — they were the only architecture she had found that kept her functional. And each time a trigger arrived — the floor supervisor's footsteps, the sound of a door clicking shut — it did not merely surface the memory; it delivered a verdict. In those moments Linh became certain, all over again, that she was permanently damaged, that ordinary life was not something she would ever be allowed to inhabit without terror.

The call center environment has become one of the most difficult spaces in her life to navigate. Male supervisors are a constant presence, and the open floor plan offers no clear escape. On days when a manager stops near her station, the fragmented memories surface with particular force — the taste returning first, then the physical sense of confinement — and Linh finds herself scanning the room for the nearest door while still speaking to a customer. These intrusions, arriving unbidden and feeling more real than the present moment, drive her toward the strategies she has come to rely on: she deflects any conversation that edges toward the assault, refuses to acknowledge it when her husband or a coworker inadvertently references something adjacent to it, and has increasingly used sexual fantasy as a way of reclaiming a sense of control over her own body. She understood, on some level, that this last strategy was not resolution — but it temporarily quieted what nothing else could.

What Linh had come to believe about herself was perhaps the most corrosive part of her presentation. She was certain she was inadequate — that her inability to simply move forward proved something fundamental about her character. That conviction, once settled, did not stay contained to her self-image — it bled outward into how she read the world. Having concluded she was broken and that danger was permanent, she moved through ordinary days as though they were mined: a colleague's neutral glance, a shift in tone on a call, the particular way a door swung open — things she would once have registered and dismissed — now snagged and held her attention as potential signals, multiplying the range of cues that could set her off. This appraisal of herself as broken kept her from disclosing the full extent of her symptoms to her husband, which in turn kept her isolated in the very relationship that might have offered repair. She was equally certain that thinking directly about the event would undo her entirely — that if she allowed the memories to surface fully rather than in pieces, she would not survive the experience. This conviction made the fragmented quality of the memories feel like protection, and so she never tried to integrate them, which meant they remained raw and trigger-ready. Her belief that she must be on guard at all times fed directly into her hypervigilant scanning and her startle responses, and those bodily reactions, arriving in public and at work, confirmed for her that the danger was real and ongoing — that her vigilance was justified.

The avoidance had its own costs. By keeping the memories at arm's length, Linh found they grew no smaller; the fragmented pieces continued to surface in response to an ever-widening range of cues. The strategies themselves had drawn the map of the event around her: every deflection, every conversation cut short, every room she mentally exited before she had to leave it physically became its own daily marker of what had happened, and each marker was a new potential trigger. The avoidance had grown in all directions until whole categories of ordinary experience — a performance review, a closed-door meeting, a male voice adopting a particular register — carried the charge of the original harm, not despite her efforts to contain them but partly because of them. A family gathering — her husband's relatives laughing together, children running between adults — could bring on a wave of shame and grief she could not account for to anyone present. An ambulance passing the call center window was enough to tighten the loop entirely. What finally brought her to seek help was a performance review scheduled by a new female supervisor — a routine meeting — during which Linh had a panic response so severe she had to leave the building. She sat in her car for forty minutes before she could drive. What she most fears is that she will never feel safe in an ordinary room. What she most hopes, though she said it quietly and without much conviction, is that the pieces might someday fit together into something she can live with.
